title: The Southern Taurid meteor shower will bring rare fireballs tonight
content: Night owls have the chance to spot a few dazzling fireballs as the Southern Taurid meteor shower hits peak activity. Southern Taurid meteors strike Earth’s atmosphere at about 65,000 miles per hour (104,607 kilometers per hour), making them slower and visible for longer than those produced by showers such as the Orionids . Meteors, which have particularly lengthy glowing trails, will appear to radiate from the Taurus constellation. Views are expected to be best at around midnight Thursday, with the estimated peak around 3 p.m. ET on November 5 according to EarthSky . “What makes the Taurids spectacular is that they’re rich in bright fireballs,” said Bill Cooke, head of NASA’s Meteoroid Environment Office. “There are not many of them, but when you see one, you’ll remember it. It’ll leave a brilliant streak across the sky.” Asteroids and comets leave behind debris trails as they eject bits of ice and rock while orbiting the sun. Meteor showers occur when Earth passes through those trails, causing the debris to hit Earth’s atmosphere, burn up and leave a blaze of light across the sky. While most bits of ice and rock that burn up are the size of dust grains or pebbles, fireballs arise from debris ranging from the size of a marble to that of a small boulder. These fireballs can be brighter than Venus: Some leave behind shining lines of ionized air molecules that disappear after a few seconds, while others produce smoke trails of cloudlike vapor that remain in the air for several minutes. “That can be really exciting — it’s much less common to see a fireball,” said astronomer Bethany Cobb Kung, associate professor of honors and physics at George Washington University. The Southern Taurid shower takes place annually and produces roughly five meteors per hour. They can be seen from almost anywhere in the world, except from the South Pole. With a crescent moon expected, meteors should be easier to spot. When looking for Taurid meteors, Kung suggests identifying the constellation Orion first — specifically its belt. “If you can find Orion and look to the right, that’s where Taurus is,” Kung said. “As long as you’re pointed in the general vicinity, you don’t have to be looking at exactly one part of the sky.” For an optimal viewing experience, find somewhere dark and give your eyes at least half an hour to adjust — without looking at your phone, according to Cooke. “Just look up and take in the show,” Cooke said. “It’s the simplest form of astronomy. All you need is your eyes.” The Southern Taurid meteor shower began in September and is set to end November 20. The Northern Taurid meteor shower — a separate but nearby trail of debris — began mid-October and will peak November 12, before ending December 10. The Southern Taurids take place as Earth passes through debris left by comet 2P/Encke — which has the shortest orbital period of any known comet in the solar system, at about 3.3 years. Scientists believe comet Encke was part of a larger body that broke up roughly 20,000 years ago, creating the complex responsible for the Southern and Northern Taurids, as well as at least three other meteor showers. Cooke’s work focuses on forecasting meteor showers to protect crews and spacecraft from hitting debris. While meteors this year are less frequent, the planet is predicted to pass through a denser swarm of Taurid debris in 2032, he said. “If you’re out the night of Halloween in 2032 and skies are clear, you may see lots of brilliant fireballs blazing above your head,” Cooke said. “We’re kind of in a lull before the thunderstorms occur.” With less than two months left of the year, you still have time to watch a few more meteor showers. Here are some peak dates to remember if you’re looking for another sky-gazing opportunity.

content: Colombia’s ancient seas supported an extraordinary diversity of top predators, offering clues to how life may undergo major evolutionary changes without a mass extinction. Mass extinctions have reshaped life on Earth, but they may not be the only way ecosystems undergo dramatic evolutionary change. Roughly 120 million years ago, the seas covering what is now central Colombia were home to an extraordinary mix of ancient Jurassic survivors and emerging Cretaceous predators. Fossils from this remarkably complex ecosystem suggest that some of evolution’s biggest turning points may unfold without a catastrophic mass extinction. The evidence comes from the Early Cretaceous Paja Formation near Villa de Leyva, Colombia, where the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) houses most of the formation’s fossils. The research at McGill University and CIP was conducted by PhD graduate Dirley Cortés and Professor Hans Larsson of McGill’s Department of Biology. “This geological formation has produced an exceptionally rich fossil record that includes giant marine reptiles like long-necked plesiosaurs and marine crocodile relatives, as well as turtles, sharks, crustaceans and others,” Cortés explained. “Together, these animals formed the Paja Biota, one of the most ecologically complex marine communities found to date.” In a previous study , the researchers estimated the Paja Biota’s food web, the network of feeding relationships among its animals. They found it was among the most complex ever to have evolved, with a high diversity of apex predators, animals at the top of the food chain. “The Paja Formation records an extraordinary process in the history of life, when a ‘perfect storm’ of environmental factors we know to promote ecological complexity coincided with ancient lineages that were about to disappear. At the same time, new groups were beginning to flourish,” Larsson said. The researchers suspect that greenhouse temperatures, high sea levels, and nutrient-rich coastal waters helped support this exceptional biodiversity and biological transition. New marine connections between the eastern Pacific and early Atlantic oceans through what is now Colombia were probably also part of that rare convergence. Many of these same factors help drive biodiversity today, they noted. Cortés and Larsson propose calling the pattern a “Biotic Inflection,” a period when many evolutionary lineages nearing extinction coexist with newly emerging groups that later diversify. “I think we’ve discovered a new model of global biodiversity change. Now we’ll need to see just how widespread this could be in Earth’s history and how we can quantify its impacts,” Larsson said. Testing the proposal will require additional fossil sampling, more precise dating, and comparisons with deposits elsewhere in the world. Those investigations would help establish how widespread the Biotic Inflection pattern was and when similar events may have occurred in Earth’s history. Reference: “The Paja Formation of Colombia records uniquely high biodiversity during a biotic inflection in an Early Cretaceous Gondwanan marine ecosystem” by Dirley Cortés and Hans C. E. Larsson, 15 May 2026, Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution . The discovery of an extraordinary mix of ancient Jurassic survivors and emerging Cretaceous predators in Colombia's Paja Formation offers a unique window into the history of life on Earth, and the findings have implications for our understanding of ecological complexity and the factors that promote it.

title: SpaceX signs deal with Qualcomm to provide network technology for U.S. mobile service
content: SpaceX announced a deal with chipmaker Qualcomm to provide key network technology for Elon Musk's Starlink Mobile service, a challenger to Verizon , AT&T and T-Mobile . Qualcomm said on Wednesday that the terrestrial network it will help SpaceX build will "complement Starlink's satellite capabilities," with a planned rollout to begin next year. Financial terms of the multiyear deal weren't disclosed. "Together with SpaceX, we are building world-leading cellular infrastructure in the United States, advancing 5G today, with an opportunity to lay the foundation for AI-native 6G in the years ahead," Durga Malladi, an executive vice president at Qualcomm, said in the statement. Starlink is a critical piece of SpaceX's business, accounting for 36% of the company's revenue in the third quarter and 85% of its operating profit. But to date, the company's consumer business has been limited when it comes to mobile direct-to-device services as its satellite network can't provide all the voice, video and data coverage that competitors offer on popular smartphones. Now SpaceX is snapping up spectrum and forging partnerships to take on the major mobile carriers. Last month, the company announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio in the 800 MHz band. The news sent shares of U.S. carriers reeling. Earlier this week, the Washington Post reported that SpaceX is in talks to acquire EchoStar's Boost Mobile. SpaceX went public in June in the largest IPO on record and is now valued at close to $2 trillion. With Qualcomm, SpaceX will be using the chipmaker's Dragonwing cellular infrastructure hardware and software in base stations to enable high-capacity coverage for Starlink Mobile. Qualcomm has a long history of making chips for cellular networks, but is best known for making the modems and radios that go inside devices, not base stations for running a wireless network. The company has targeted carriers and other infrastructure companies since it made a bigger push into the 5G infrastructure market in 2020 . SpaceX represents one of Qualcomm's highest-profile customers or partners in 5G infrastructure, following earlier deals with Verizon, Dish, and Europe's Vodafone. While SpaceX plans to use Qualcomm's technology to establish tens of thousands of new cell sites, it hasn't announced partners among cell tower companies or said how many new towers may be required. Mobile carriers generally lease space from companies such as American Tower and Crown Castle , which commonly host multiple carriers from one site. SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's request for additional information. -- CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed reporting. WATCH: SpaceX most undervalued opportunity
